newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia talks tough ahead of NATO leader's visit.
newsitem.headline: Russia talks tough ahead of NATO leader's visit.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin has told his top negotiator to take a tough line in talks with NATO on Tuesday despite signs Moscow may be ready to sign a security agreement with the Western defence alliance on May 27.

Itar-Tass news agency said Yeltsin had instructed Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov to take a firm line in defending Russia's interests at Tuesday's meeting in Moscow with NATO Secretary General Javier Solana.

"The president confirmed the foreign minister's mandate for the talks and noted the need to continue the firm Russian line, based on defending the country's interests especially on...military questions," Tass said, quoting presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky.

Solana was due to arrive in Moscow on Tuesday afternoon for the talks which Primakov says will decide whether Russia and NATO can sign an agreement on a peaceful new relationship after years of mistrust.

Some Kremlin sources say Russia has already decided to sign the deal in Paris on May 27, but intends to keep up the uncertainty and anti-NATO rhetoric until the last minute to appease domestic opponents who fear Yeltsin is selling out national interests.

Yeltsin discussed security matters on Tuesday with West German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and new British Prime Minister Tony Blair, continuing what the Kremlin says will be several days of telephone diplomacy with NATO leaders.

Yeltsin, who spoke to French President Jacques Chirac on Monday, agreed with Kohl that "maximum constructiveness" was needed to solve the remaining problems, Interfax news agency quoted the presidential press service as saying.
The Moscow-NATO deal is intended to overcome Russia's strong objections to the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's plans to expand to take in new members from the former Soviet bloc.
Solana, who last met Primakov in Luxembourg last week, was expected to keep a low public profile when he arrived in Moscow and not to meet reporters.
Yeltsin does not plan to meet Solana but may telephone him during his stay in Moscow, Yastrzhembsky said.
The president called U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright midway during her talks with Primakov earlier this month and had a lengthy telephone conversation although he did not meet her.

The main disagreements over a deal defining a new partnership between the former Cold War foes include Moscow's demands for written guarantees that the alliance will not move its military might into new member states.
Russia is also demanding progress over amending a 1990 treaty governing conventional arms in Europe and a say in decision-making on security issues.
NATO has ruled out a Russian "veto". A planned joint Russia-NATO council appears likely only to give Moscow a say in consultations on matters affecting its own security.
Invitations to new NATO members are due to go out at an alliance summit in Madrid in July.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are thought be the leading contenders to join NATO, but Romania and Slovenia also hope to be in the first wave of new members.
